worgle-answer-today.articleHtml:
Welsh throws most solvers off balance within the first two guesses. The alphabet behaves differently here—letters that sit dormant in English dominate Welsh vocabulary, and patterns that look wrong are often exactly right.

Worgle answer today: what the Welsh letter pattern is hinting at

The answer card on today's page reveals a five-letter Welsh word using several high-frequency Welsh consonants. How to read common Welsh digraphs without overforcing them

Welsh digraphs like CH, DD, LL, NG, RH, and TH each count as single sounds but occupy two letter spaces on the board. This trips up players who treat every two-letter pair as separate entities. A word containing "DD" isn't broken—the DD is one phoneme representing a voiced dental fricative, roughly like saying "this" but softer.

When scanning the clue widgets on today's board, watch for these patterns:

  • CH appears frequently in position three or four, especially after vowels
  • DD almost never starts a valid Welsh word but shows up mid-vocabulary regularly
  • LL clusters appear in structurally similar ways to English double-L words

The solver linked on this page can validate whether a potential guess follows Welsh orthographic rules. Don't rely on English intuition—when in doubt, run it through the tool rather than burning a guess on a pattern that doesn't exist in Welsh.

Where English guessing habits break the solve

Most players approach Worgle with Wordle muscle memory. That works until it doesn't. English favors J, K, Q, X, and Z in specific contexts; Welsh barely uses them. If your opening guesses loaded up on those letters expecting coverage, you've wasted slots on tiles that simply won't appear.

Y behaves completely differently too. In English, Y usually acts as a vowel substitute. In Welsh, Y is a full vowel with two distinct pronunciations depending on stress and position—it can sound like uh, ee, or even disappear entirely in fast speech. Seeing Y highlighted yellow on the board doesn't mean you've misread anything. It means the word contains that vowel in a position where Welsh allows it.

Build your starting list around Welsh-friendly consonants before you ever see the board. Why does Welsh use so many doubled letters?

Double letters in Welsh serve phonological purposes rather than emphasis. LL represents a voiceless alveolar lateral fricative—a sound English lacks entirely. DD marks a voiced equivalent. These aren't stylistic choices; they're distinct phonemes that change meaning. Treating DD as two separate letters misses the point entirely.
